acts.title: Salt Road (2023) ★★★★☆
text: Some films get better on a second watch. Salt Road, the first feature by Aliya Bekova, is one of them.

The story is simple. A retired driver agrees to take a stranger four hundred kilometres across the steppe to a wedding he has not been invited to. That is essentially the whole plot, and it is enough.

The performances are what carry it. The two leads spend most of the film in the front seats of an old van, and neither of them explains anything. The photography is absolutely stunning — the long shots of the salt flats at sunset are worth the ticket on their own — and the soundtrack is quiet enough to let you hear the engine.

It is not perfect. The middle half-hour is rather slow, and one scene at the petrol station is frankly infuriating: we are told something we had already worked out for ourselves twenty minutes earlier.
On balance, though, this is nowhere near as heavy as it sounds. It is essentially a comedy about two people who are bad at talking to each other.
If you want special effects, don’t bother. If you have two quiet hours, I’d definitely recommend it — and it’s well worth seeing on a big screen.

write.q: Write a review of about 200 words of a film, a game or a series you know well. Follow the model: hook → plot without spoilers → what works, with evidence → what does not work → weighing up → what the reader should do.
write.model:
Some series are better watched slowly, one episode a week, and this is one of them.

The idea is small. A retired teacher in a mining town starts answering the letters that arrive for the previous owner of her flat. She has never met any of the people writing them. That is essentially the whole story.

What carries it is the performances. The lead is on screen for almost every minute and never raises her voice. The writing is quietly, absolutely brilliant: three or four lines an episode that you think about the next day. The soundtrack is unusually restrained.

It is not perfect. The fourth episode is rather slow, and the storyline about the son is frankly infuriating — we work it out long before anybody on screen does.

On balance, though, it is nowhere near as sad as the first episode suggests. It is essentially a comedy about a woman who is very bad at minding her own business.

If you want something fast, don’t bother. Otherwise I’d definitely recommend it. The best part is that it ends properly, which almost nothing does any more.

speak.q: Now do it out loud, as a conversation. Somebody asks whether they should watch it. Compare it with something else they know, name the best part, and give a clear recommendation.
speak.model: Should you watch it? Yes — but not all in one night. It’s nowhere near as sad as the first episode makes it look; it’s essentially a comedy. The best part is the writing: three or four lines an episode that stay with you. The fourth episode is slow, I’ll admit. On balance, though, I’d definitely recommend it. And it actually ends properly, which is rare.
